name: Accenture (ASE & Advanced ASE)
tagline: Cognitive, technical, coding and communication assessments

overview.about: Accenture hires engineering freshers mainly as Associate Software Engineer (ASE), with a higher-package Advanced ASE track for strong coders. The process combines a cognitive & technical assessment, a coding assessment, an AI-scored communication assessment and an interview. Recent cycles report game-based cognitive items. Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.
eligibility: Typically 60% or more (or equivalent) in 10th, 12th/diploma and graduation (as reported)
No active backlogs at joining; gap rules per notice

cards.title: Cognitive assessment
cards.body: Critical reasoning (arithmetic word problems, logical deductions), abstract reasoning (patterns, series, odd-one-out, matrices) and English (RC, grammar, vocabulary). Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.

points: Pseudo-code output tracing
MS Office & common applications (Excel functions, Word, PowerPoint)

cards.title: Cloud basics in one card
points: IaaS: rent VMs/storage (e.g. EC2-type services)
PaaS: platform to deploy code without managing servers
SaaS: finished software over the web (email, CRM)
Public / private / hybrid cloud

cards.title: Security basics
cards.body: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key (AES); asymmetric uses a public/private pair (RSA). Phishing is social engineering; a firewall filters traffic by rules.

cards.title: MS Office style
cards.body:
Q: Which Excel function returns the number of non-empty cells in A1:A10?
COUNTA(A1:A10). COUNT counts only numeric cells.

cards.title: Game-based items
cards.body: If you get game-style cognitive tasks, read instructions fully — practice rounds don't count. Accuracy usually matters more than raw speed.

cards.q: Web email delivered to users over the internet is an example of:
cards.explain: Users consume finished software; the provider manages everything.

cards.q: Which encryption uses a public/private key pair?
cards.explain: Base64 isn't encryption; hashing is one-way.

cards.q: Excel: count numeric cells only in A1:A10:
cards.explain: COUNT counts numbers; COUNTA counts any non-empty cell.

notes.p: Accenture's fresher hiring (for roles such as **Associate Software Engineer**) usually starts with a **Cognitive and Technical Assessment** of roughly 90 questions in about 90 minutes. It is commonly an **elimination round**: you must clear it to reach coding and communication rounds. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.
points: **Cognitive:** English ability, critical reasoning and problem solving, abstract reasoning.
**Technical:** common applications and MS Office, pseudo-code, fundamentals of networking, security and cloud.
No negative marking has been reported, but there is little time — about a minute per question.

notes.p:
**MS Office.** Which Excel function counts non-empty cells? **COUNTA** (COUNT counts only numbers). Shortcut for a new slide in PowerPoint? **Ctrl + M**. In Word, Ctrl + E? **Centre-aligns** text. Which Excel feature summarises large data by categories? **Pivot table**.

**Networking.** Which protocol finds a MAC address from an IP address? **ARP**. Which device connects different networks? **Router**. Default HTTPS port? **443**.

**Security.** An email pretending to be your bank and asking for your password is **phishing**. Malware that encrypts files and demands payment is **ransomware**. Two-factor authentication combines something you know with something you have.

**Cloud.** Gmail is **SaaS**; a platform where you deploy code without managing servers (like Google App Engine) is **PaaS**; renting virtual machines (like AWS EC2) is **IaaS**.

**Pseudo-code.** `set n = 6, s = 0; while n > 0: if n mod 2 == 0 then s = s + n; n = n - 1; print s`. It adds the even numbers 6, 4, 2 → **12**.

**Critical reasoning.** 'Sales rose after the advertising campaign, so the campaign caused the rise.' Which weakens it? An option like 'A competitor shut down in the same month' — it gives another cause.

**Abstract reasoning.** Look for one change at a time across figures: rotation (45° or 90° steps), count of shapes, shading moving one position, or an element added each step.

**English.** 'He has been working here since five years.' Correct: **for five years** (for a duration; 'since' needs a point in time).

`n, s = 6, 0
while n > 0:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        s += n
    n -= 1
print(s)`

Output:
`12`

points: Revise MS Office shortcuts and common Excel functions (SUM, COUNTIF, VLOOKUP, IF) — easy marks often skipped.
Learn one-line definitions of cloud models, common attacks (phishing, DDoS, SQL injection) and OSI layers.
For abstract reasoning, check rotation, count and shading in that order.
Move on after a minute; there is little time for review.
Take at least two full mocks in the same timing.
Confusing COUNT and COUNTA, or IaaS and PaaS.
Reading 'which is NOT' questions as 'which is'.
Over-reading critical reasoning options — pick the one that directly affects the argument.
Elimination round: cognitive + technical.
Office: COUNTA, pivot tables, Ctrl + M, Ctrl + E.
Network: ARP, router, 443.
Security: phishing, ransomware, 2FA.
Cloud: SaaS (Gmail), PaaS (deploy code), IaaS (VMs).
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Coding assessment
cards.body: Two problems, about 45 minutes. Function-based or full-program style. Typical topics: arrays, strings, simple math, sorting, occasionally basic DP. One fully passing solution is the usual minimum.

cards.title: Typical problem
Communication assessment
cards.body: Speaking and listening tasks: read sentences aloud, repeat what you hear, answer short questions. Scored on pronunciation, fluency and grammar by software.

cards.title: Communication tips
cards.body: Use a quiet room and wired headset; speak at a steady pace; don't restart sentences. A clear neutral accent beats speed.

cards.title: Interview
cards.body: Usually one combined technical + HR round: your project, a language of choice, OOP, DBMS, a basic program, cloud awareness, and willingness to relocate/work in shifts.

cards.title: Advanced ASE
cards.body: A higher-package track for candidates who perform strongly in an additional/advanced coding assessment and interview. Check the current notice for how it is offered.

cards.q: solve([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) with the 'odd values at even indices' rule returns:
For an AI-scored speaking test, what helps most?
options: Steady pace, clear pronunciation, quiet room
cards.explain: Fluency and clarity are what the scoring measures.

notes.p: Candidates who clear the first assessment are reported to get a **coding round with 2 problems in about 45 minutes**. Problems are often **function-based**: you complete a given function that receives parameters and returns a value, rather than reading input yourself. Clearing at least one problem fully is commonly needed; solving both improves your chances. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

**Problem 1.** Complete `sum_greater(arr, num)`: return the sum of elements greater than `num`; return 0 if none; return -1 if the array is empty.

**Problem 2.** Complete `reverse_words(s)`: reverse each word but keep the word order.

`def sum_greater(arr, num):
    if not arr:
        return -1
    return sum(x for x in arr if x > num)

def reverse_words(s):
    return " ".join(w[::-1] for w in s.split(" "))

print(sum_greater([4, 9, 1, 12, 7], 6))
print(sum_greater([1, 2], 5), sum_greater([], 5))
print(reverse_words("hello world from accenture"))`

Output:
`28
0 -1
olleh dlrow morf erutnecca`

Read the special cases carefully — 'return -1 for an empty array' is exactly the kind of hidden test case that fails careless solutions. Both functions run in O(n).

An automated spoken-English test checks **pronunciation, fluency, grammar, vocabulary and listening**. Typical tasks reported: reading sentences aloud, repeating sentences you hear, answering short questions, building sentences from jumbled phrases, retelling a short story and speaking on an open question.
points: Use a quiet room and a good headset; test your microphone first.
Speak at a steady, natural pace — do not rush.
If you miss a word in a repeat task, say the rest smoothly instead of stopping.
For story retelling, cover who, what happened and how it ended.
Practise daily by reading news aloud and recording yourself.

notes.p:
**Q: Tell me about yourself.** A: Present (degree, key skills), past (project/internship with a result), future (why this role).

**Q: What is cloud computing?** A: On-demand computing resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing; models are IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

**Q: Explain OOP with an example from your project.** A: Name a class you built, how you encapsulated data, and where inheritance or polymorphism helped.

**Q: Why Accenture?** A: Mention its consulting plus technology mix, varied client industries and learning programmes, and connect to your goals.

**Q: Are you comfortable with any technology and location?** A: Answer honestly and show flexibility.
Where candidates lose the coding round:
points: Changing the given function name or signature — the judge calls it exactly as given.
Printing the answer instead of returning it in function-based problems.
Ignoring null/empty inputs and negative numbers.
Spending all 45 minutes on one problem; time-box the first one to about 20 minutes.
Coding: about 2 function-based problems in about 45 minutes.
Handle empty/null and 'no result' cases exactly as stated.
Communication test is automated — clarity and pace matter.
Interview: project, OOP, cloud basics, HR.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.
